The wrecks recede rank on rank into the distance, the nearer hulls sharp and the far ones dissolving into a grey haze of countless drifting dead.
A colossal flagship hull dominates the field, kilometers long, smaller wrecks drifting around its broken bulk like minnows around a dead whale of steel.
The boneyard stretches past a dead grey moon, thousands of hulls dwindling to a glittering band of specks against the stars.
A wreck so enormous its hull curves away at the edges like terrain, horizon to horizon nothing but pitted grey metal and shattered superstructure.
Canyon walls of stacked debris rise on either side, broken hulls compressed into cliffs, the passage between them dark and impossibly deep.
The field fills the viewport edge to edge, no stars visible, only wreckage layered upon wreckage in every direction without end.
Thousands of hulls diminish in perfect recession until the farthest are mere bright points, indistinguishable from the stars they drift against.
Layer upon layer of debris fades into atmospheric haze, the nearer wrecks crisp, the distant ones pale ghosts dissolving into blue-grey nothing.
The graveyard extends so far that curvature claims the horizon, the outermost wrecks bending gently downward and out of sight over the planetary rim.
Smaller ships cluster against a shattered dreadnought like barnacles on a sea-cliff, the dreadnought itself vanishing into haze kilometers ahead.
Depth upon depth of drifting dead, each successive layer dimmer and more spectral, the farthest wrecks barely distinguishable from cold background radiation.
The flagship's broken spine stretches so long that its far end is a different shade, atmospheric scatter turning steel into grey suggestion.
Wreck behind wreck behind wreck, the boneyard stacked in three dimensions, every sight-line terminated by another hull rather than open space.
A single lateral sweep of the viewport takes several full seconds before the field's edge appears, and then does not appear.
Debris plumes stream outward from the central carnage like the arms of a galaxy, each arm thick with tumbling hulls beyond counting.
The nearest wreck dwarfs the observation deck entirely, yet behind it three more loom larger still, and behind those the field simply continues.
Looking down into the graveyard from above is like looking into an ocean of metal, depth vanishing into darkness long before a bottom appears.
A frigate hull, itself enormous, is pinned beneath a cruiser's fallen drive section the way a pebble is pinned beneath a boot.
The grid of wreckage extends past the terminator of the dead moon and presumably onward, the far side unexamined and equally full.
Counting becomes absurd; the eye simply stops attempting and accepts vastness, accepting that thousands is a floor and not a ceiling.
Scattered lights of still-cycling emergency beacons mark the field in every direction, a constellation of catastrophe stretching to the limit of vision.
A debris field so dense it casts a shadow across the planet below, a moving dark stain visible from the surface as a second twilight.
The wreck at the center is not a ship anymore but a geography, a range of broken metal peaks with valleys and ravines between.
Even at full thrust it takes three hours to cross from one edge of the graveyard to the other, and that is only one axis.
The oldest wrecks at the field's heart are compressed by collision into abstract masses, centuries of drift having erased all sense of their original scale.
